zydeco.e: From Louisiana Creole zydéco, compare French zarico; possibly from a metanalysis of French les haricots (“beans”) as French le zarico (“beans”) in a dance-tune title.

s.d: music of southern Louisiana that combines French dance melodies with Caribbean music and blues
(uncountable) A form of Louisiana Creole music, characteristically performed by accordion and washboard bands, that combines Cajun and Creole roots music with elements of African-American music.
x: Sunpie—in real life, a park ranger and an accordionist who leads a good zydeco band—taunted Harrison […].

s.d: Any bird with toes of this kind, such as the parrot.
(of bird feet) having the first and fourth toes directed backward the second and third forward
Having two toes pointing forward, and two pointing backward; zygodactylous.
x: In parrots, the tarsometatarsus has a distinct shape resulting from the particular arrangement of parrot toes. As zygodactyl birds, toes number 2 and 3 are facing forward, while toes 1 and 4 are facing backwards.

s.d: a bird's foot having the first and fourth toes of each foot directed backward and the second and third forward

zygoma.e: From Ancient Greek ζύγωμα (zúgōma), from ζυγόν (zugón, “yoke”), a connector for joining animals.

s.d: the slender arch formed by the temporal process of the cheekbone that bridges to the zygomatic process of the temporal bone
The cheekbone.
the arch of bone beneath the eye that forms the prominence of the cheek
of or relating to the cheek region of the face
Of, relating to, or located in the area of the zygomatic bone or zygomatic arch.
x: They show (1) the left orbit and zygomatic arch of President Kennedy magnified from Zapruder frame 230

s.d: the slender arch formed by the temporal process of the cheekbone that bridges to the zygomatic process of the temporal bone
the arch of bone beneath the eye that forms the prominence of the cheek
The cheekbone.
a slender process of the temporal bone that strengthens the zygomatic arch
A protrusion from the rest of the skull, most of it belonging to the zygomatic bone, but also contributed to by the frontal bone, maxilla and temporal bone.
capable of division into symmetrical halves by only one longitudinal plane passing through the axis
Having bilateral symmetry.
capable of division into symmetrical halves by only one longitudinal plane passing through the axis
zygomorphic
a plant spore formed by two similar sexual cells
A zygosperm.
A spore formed by the union of several zoospores.

zygote.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ζῠγωτός (zŭgōtós, “yoked”) + English -ote (suffix meaning ‘having [the thing to which it is attached]’). Ζῠγωτός (Zŭgōtós) is derived from ζῠγόω (zŭgóō, “to join or yoke together”) + -τός (-tós, suffix forming adjectives of possibility); and ζῠγόω (zŭgóō) from ζῠγόν (zŭgón, “yoke for joining animals; anything which joins two things together”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *yewg- (“to tie together, join, yoke”)) + -όω (-óō, suffix forming causative or f

s.d: (genetics) the diploid cell resulting from the union of a haploid spermatozoon and ovum (including the organism that develops from that cell)
A eukaryotic cell formed from the fusion of two gametes (“reproductive cells”) during a fertilization process.

zygotene.e:
From French zygotène, corresponding to zygo- (“union, zygosis”, from Ancient Greek ζυγόν (zugón, “junction, yoke”)) + -tene (“filament”, from ταινία (tainía, “band, fillet”)), equivalent to zygote + -tene.
Coined by Victor Grégoire in 1907 and in English by Edmund B. Wilson in 1912.

s.d: the second stage of the prophase of meiosis
The intimate pairing of homologous chromosomes during the synaptic stage of meiosis

Old French -iquebor.

From zygote + -ic.

s.d: of or relating to a zygote
Of, pertaining to or existing as a zygote.
a complex of enzymes that cause glycolysis; originally found in yeast but also present in higher organisms
(uncountable) Any of a group of enzymes that catalyze the fermentation of simple carbohydrates to ethanol and carbon dioxide.

A proenzyme, or enzyme precursor, which requires a biochemical change (i.e. hydrolysis) to become an active form of the enzyme.
resembling an enzyme
(obsolete) Resembling a zymin or ferment (enzyme)

zymology.e: From zymo- (prefix meaning ‘fermentation’) + -logy (suffix denoting the study of a particular subject).

s.d: the branch of chemistry concerned with fermentation (as in making wine or brewing or distilling)
(uncountable) The chemistry of fermentation with yeasts, especially the science involved in beermaking and winemaking; zymurgy.
(uncountable) A treatise on the use of fermentation to produce liquors.
a process in which an agent causes an organic substance to break down into simpler substances; especially, the anaerobic breakdown of sugar into alcohol
(uncountable) The action of enzymes in breaking down organic substances during fermentation
of or relating to or causing fermentation
a process in which an agent causes an organic substance to break down into simpler substances; especially, the anaerobic breakdown of sugar into alcohol
(medicine) the development and spread of an infectious disease (especially one caused by a fungus)
(uncountable) A fermentation
(obsolete, uncountable) A process by which an infectious disease is believed to be developed, seen as similar to the process of fermentation, and caused by so-called microzymes, also known as zymes.
(obsolete, uncountable) A zymotic disease.

zymotic.e: From Ancient Greek ζυμωτικός (zumōtikós, “causing fermentation”), from ζυμοῦν (zumoûn).

s.d: of or relating to or causing fermentation
relating to or caused by infection
(historical) Infectious, contagious, of diseases originally regarded as being caused by a process similar to fermentation.
x: Farr concluded that overcrowding was the main determinant of high mortality from what (following Liebig) he style ‘zymotic diseases’.

zymurgy.e: From zym- (prefix meaning ‘fermentation’) + -urgy (suffix denoting a technique for working with something), modelled after metallurgy.

s.d: the branch of chemistry concerned with fermentation (as in making wine or brewing or distilling)
(uncountable) Synonym of zymology (“the chemistry of fermentation with yeasts, especially the science involved in beermaking and winemaking”).
x: The natural languages, however, cover every subject from aardvarks to zymurgies.
Going by the amount of liquor you consume, I thought the only science that interested you was zymurgy, which would make you an illegal scientist because you are not quite eighteen yet.

s.d: (uncountable) The practice of using fermentation to produce alcoholic beverages.
x: Of Zymurgy I little know, / Perhaps because I little knead, / And can but make a sorry show / In singing liaisons of feed, / Flour, fodder,— […]
